title: Isandro and the Radiators
premise: Sable Voss has spent nine years writing postcards to the Radiator House, a boarding home that burned down with three people inside, mailing them to an address that no longer exists. When a demolition crew tears open a wall and finds a box of undelivered letters — including Sable's own, returned unopened by a postal worker who never sent them back — Sable is forced to confront Halcyon Marsh, the house's former caretaker who everyone believes died in the fire but who actually escaped and has been living quietly nearby. As Sable pieces together the night of the fire through the letters' overlapping voices, they discover the blaze was set to destroy evidence of the house's benefactor's crimes against its residents, and that Halcyon took the blame to protect the children who actually started it. The story ends with Sable choosing to publish the letters rather than preserve their own careful silence, giving the dead their names back while letting Halcyon finally be seen.
about_author: Xanthe Dunmore is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing undelivered mail for a municipal records office. They write about the paper trails people leave behind and the courage it takes to read them aloud.

chapters.title: The Inventory of Unsaid Things
chapters.summary: Sable Voss, a professional letter-writer who composes other people's difficult words, writes postcard number 312 to the burned Radiator House. POV: Sable. Establishes Sable's ritual of saying everything to an address that cannot answer, and the emotional beat of devotion disguised as habit.

chapters.title: What the Demolition Crew Found
chapters.summary: A crew tearing down the last standing wall of the Radiator House uncovers a tin box wedged behind a wardrobe: forty-one letters, all addressed to residents, none ever delivered. POV: Sable, arriving at the site. The beat is vertigo — the past physically surfacing into the present.

chapters.title: Return to Sender
chapters.summary: Sable recognizes their own handwriting among the letters and learns from retired postman Ede Lark that he kept them back deliberately, unable to deliver mail to the dead. POV: Ede. His guilt reframes Sable's ritual: someone else was also writing to the ashes, in his own way.

chapters.title: The Woman at the Bus Stop
chapters.summary: Sable spots a woman whose face matches a photograph found tucked in the letter box — Halcyon Marsh, the caretaker listed as dead. She flees before Sable can speak. POV: Sable. The beat is the first crack in the official story; the dead may be walking.

chapters.title: Letters to Juniper
chapters.summary: Sable reads the earliest letters, written to a girl named Juniper by her mother outside the house, full of small domestic love and mounting worry. POV: alternating epistolary voices filtered through Sable. The beat is tenderness curdling toward dread as the mother's questions go unanswered.

chapters.title: The Benefactor's Generosity
chapters.summary: A letter from the house's wealthy founder, Corwin Ashe, reveals his patronage — and his insistence on privacy, on doors locked at night, on residents who 'owe discretion.' POV: Sable reading. The beat is the slow recognition that charity can be a cage.

chapters.title: Halcyon, Alive
chapters.summary: Sable tracks Halcyon to a laundromat where she works nights. She neither confirms nor denies her identity but says: 'You don't want to know what I let them believe.' POV: Halcyon, her first interior chapter. The beat is exhaustion — a woman tired of being a ghost.

chapters.title: Three Names Missing
chapters.summary: Cross-referencing the letters with the fire report, Sable finds only two victims named though three beds were accounted for. A third resident, a boy called Tam, vanished from every record. POV: Sable. The beat is archival horror — someone has been erased twice, once by fire, once by paperwork.

chapters.title: Juniper's Last Letter
chapters.summary: The final undelivered letter, written the week of the fire, is from Juniper herself — not received but drafted, describing something she saw through the benefactor's unlocked study door. POV: Juniper via the letter, framed by Sable. The beat is a child's clarity cutting through adult euphemism.

chapters.title: Ede Confesses
chapters.summary: Ede admits he withheld the letters because one of them implicated a man the whole town still honors, and delivering it would have burned more than a house. POV: Ede. The beat is complicity — justice delayed by ordinary decency twisted into cowardice.

chapters.title: The Night It Burned
chapters.summary: Halcyon begins her account: the fire started in the study, where the older children had gathered Ashe's ledgers documenting what he did to Tam. She shepherded them out and went back for the box. POV: Halcyon. The beat is terror transmuted into resolve.

chapters.title: What Halcyon Let Them Believe
chapters.summary: Halcyon explains she was reported dead because the children needed the story closed — a dead caretaker meant no investigation, no questions to children already broken. POV: Halcyon. The beat is the terrible arithmetic of protection: her life traded for their silence.

chapters.title: Corwin Ashe Still Stands
chapters.summary: Sable discovers Ashe is alive, elderly, philanthropic, his name on a new wing of the town library. POV: Sable, attending a dedication ceremony. The beat is cold fury — power outliving its crimes, wearing marble.

chapters.title: The Children, Grown
chapters.summary: Sable locates two of the now-adult residents, one a nurse, one in prison, both still bound by the old pact. One begs Sable to stop; the other slips them a key. POV: split between Sable and brief secondhand testimony. The beat is belonging as both wound and chain.

chapters.title: The Key
chapters.summary: The key opens a storage unit holding Tam's belongings — and a ledger page proving Ashe falsified Tam's death record years before the fire. POV: Sable. The beat is dread sharpening into purpose: Tam didn't die in the fire; he died before it, or was made to disappear.

chapters.title: Ashe Sends for Sable
chapters.summary: Ashe, alerted by the demolition, invites Sable to his estate and offers money for the letters, speaking of 'closure' and 'moving forward.' POV: Sable. The beat is temptation as threat — corruption offering itself politely, with tea.

chapters.title: Halcyon Decides
chapters.summary: Halcyon tells Sable she will testify, ending her ghosthood, but only if the letters are published whole — including the parts that shame the children. POV: Halcyon. The beat is the cost of truth priced honestly, and accepted.

chapters.title: The Fire Again
chapters.summary: Ashe's lawyer files to seize the letters as 'estate property'; that night the storage unit burns. Sable saves the ledger page and nothing else. POV: Sable. The beat is escalation — the past repeating its method, and failing this time.

chapters.title: Reading Aloud
chapters.summary: In the library wing bearing Ashe's name, Sable reads the letters publicly, one by one, while Halcyon stands beside them, alive and named. POV: Sable. The climax: justice enacted not by law but by witness, voice, and audience.

chapters.title: Tam
chapters.summary: The reading draws out an old groundskeeper who reveals where Tam really went — sent away, alive then, to an institution Ashe controlled. Sable finds Tam's trail, decades cold but not erased. POV: Sable and the groundskeeper. The beat is grief with a direction at last.

chapters.title: Postcard 313
chapters.summary: Ashe is indicted on document fraud; the case for worse charges builds slowly, imperfectly. Sable mails postcard 313 — to Halcyon's real address, which Halcyon gave them. POV: Sable. The beat is ritual transformed: the same act, now aimed at the living.

chapters.title: Everything Said
chapters.summary: Spring. The letters are published as a book; Juniper's mother reads her daughter's words at the grave. Sable, whose inventory of unsaid things once defined them, writes nothing unsent anymore. POV: Sable. The resolution: belonging rebuilt on truth, silence spent at last.
